item.title: I left my wife and twins behind - why this Nigerian man fled South Africa
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gx2y454w5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
I left my wife and twins behind - why this Nigerian man fled South Africa - Published Nigerian Richard Itoro is not sure when he will see his twin children again. Fearing for his safety as the anti-migrant protests cranked up in South Africa this year, the 47-year-old left his family and business behind in Johannesburg and boarded one of the voluntary repatriation flights to Nigeria in June. His is just one of many experiences that is fuelling diplomatic tension and threatening to rupture relations between South Africa and other countries on the continent. Tens of thousands of foreigners have left the country over the past two months. "It was painful for me to leave [the] person who's my best friend," Itoro tells the BBC, with tears welling up, as he reflects on saying goodbye to his South African wife. Over 15 years, he had built up a car-dealership business, bought a home and created a family. That is now all gone for him. Itoro became the target of harassment but his wife was not spared the intimidation. He says his neighbours told her: "You're married to a Nigerian. Those of you who are married to Nigerians we are supposed to arrest you people. "You guys betrayed us. Go and leave the country with your husband and don't be here." Itoro was baffled. "My family was just a small family, which was beautiful and peaceful. I had no issues with anybody." The pressure became too much. "If I go home and start all over again, it's better than being here, being harassed, being scared for my life," Itoro says. But, the businessman says, the Nigerian high commission would not let his wife and children travel with him. He describes how leaving felt like a movie where someone boards the last helicopter flight out of a besieged city. "I wish I could have just begged the people from the embassy and said: 'This is my wife, I can't leave her behind and my kids,' but I couldn't. "So my car started departing and I wished I had told her not to cry." The anti-migrant groups in South Africa said their protests were aimed at undocumented foreigners. The country's outspoken Culture Minister, Gayton McKenzie, who leads one of the parties in the coalition government, also emphasised this point. "We say South Africa is open to our brothers on the continent but come here legitimately. Come with your papers," he told the BBC's Interview programme. But Itoro says his legal status did not protect him from hostility as he shows the BBC a copy of the document that he says proves he had the right to stay in the country. He was not alone, according to the Nigerian authorities. "We have records of Nigerians who have legitimate papers to remain in South Africa, yet they have been attacked," Nigeria's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Sola Enikanolaiye said during a recent meeting with South Africa's Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola. The temperature was raised last week following the death of a Nigerian who was killed as police were arresting him over suspected drug offences. An independent body is now investigating. Lamola maintained that South Africa deals with those who take the law into their own hands, but added that President Cyril Ramaphosa was also "very firm on South Africa's sovereign right to enforce its immigration laws". Despite the diplomatic efforts, South Africa's reputation has been severely damaged. Not least because of images and videos circulating on social media. Not all of them were what they were purported to be, but one, involving a Ghanaian, was genuine and it sparked huge concern once it started being shared in April. When Emmanuel Asamoah left Ghana in 2023 for South Africa, he was chasing the kind of opportunity many migrants dream about. The 37-year-old hairstylist settled in Soweto, on the outskirts of Johannesburg, found work, built a life and believed he had a future in one of Africa's biggest economies. But three months ago that future suddenly felt uncertain when he was surrounded by a group of South Africans who demanded that he leave. The confrontation was captured on video. "This thing of you guys moving from one country to another… is no longer working," one woman can be seen telling Asamoah. "Now, we are making it very clear to you guys, we don't want you here. We want you to fix your countries." Having returned to Ghana's capital, Accra, in May, Asamoah tells the BBC that the encounter left him terrified. "They came to me and started pushing me... So, they started asking questions and harassing me… they said that I should go home, that we are spoiling their country, because of us, they don't eat, we are taking their girlfriends," he says. South Africa's high jobless rate - standing at more than 30% - is seen as one of the factors fuelling the tension. It was a sentiment echoed by McKenzie. "No man can feed another man's children while his children are starving. Our people are starving of jobs," he said backing calls for those who came to the country without papers to leave. But Asamoah insists he had a stamp in his passport giving him permission to stay. "I was not illegal. I was legal in South Africa. That's why I told them that, they can take me to the police station so that we can go to Home Affairs and verify," he says. For Asamoah, returning home has brought an unexpected fresh start. With support from a Ghanaian businessman, he has opened a cement business and is determined to build his future. "My brothers and sisters in South Africa. I'm in Ghana now. I'm fixing my country," he says. But Ghana's government remains angry at the way it sees its citizens are being viewed in South Africa. In an interview with the BBC, Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa spoke about how he saw it as going against the spirit of continental solidarity and a failure to recognise how African countries helped in the struggle against apartheid, which ended in 1994. South Africa "should be the epitome of Pan-Africanism. We talk about African integration. We talk about free movement… even if you have issues with high immigration, is this how you resolve it?", the minister asked. In Lagos, Itoro is still pining for his family. "It's not easy. But we talk every day, and I'm broken. There is hope, because... my wife is going to join me very soon, as soon as God lifts me up. But it was heartbreaking, and that's how I felt: like I lost everything," he says. item.title: US states sue to block Trump tariffs impacting dozens of countries
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy4kp8jd0ppo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US states sue to block Trump tariffs impacting dozens of countries - Published Twenty-five states sued President Donald Trump's administration on Monday over a wave of tariffs against dozens of countries. The US says the tariffs, which range between 10% and 12.5%, were imposed due to trading partners - including the UK, China and the European Union - failing to properly tackle forced labour. In a legal document seen by the BBC, the coalition of Democratic states said the decision was "arbitrary, capricious, and contrary to law". In response, White House spokesman Kush Desai said the US was "using its lawful authority" to address practices that burden American businesses. Desai added that any foreign countries failing to deal with the importation of goods produced with forced labour was "unreasonable" and must be addressed. The new tariffs, which came into effect in July, were imposed under Section 301 of the 1974 US Trade Act, legislation which is designed to target nations that use forced labour. The duties cover 99.4% of US imports, according to the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR). During Trump's first term, he used Section 301 to impose trade tariffs on China and they survived challenges in court. Desai added: "Section 301 tariffs have proven to be a legally durable tool since the president's first term, and they remain so now." The lawsuit said the Trump administration "cannot use forced labour as a pretext to continue its illegal tariff scheme". "The tariffs the USTR imposed are so broad that they defy the USTR's own stated aims and make a mockery of the statute used to justify them," it said. The lawsuit added that the last time Trump used Section 301 to impose tariffs, solely targeting China in 2018, officials had investigated claims of forced labour in the country for eight months. That compares with just two months for the most recent probe, which looked into 60 trading partners, it said. "Typically, a Section 301 investigation into even a single economy takes much longer to complete," it argued. "President Trump's illegal tariffs are nothing more than a tax on hardworking families," said New York Governor Kathy Hochul. In a statement, Oregon attorney general Dan Rayfield said: "Despite losing every step of the way, Trump is trying yet again to inflict more chaos on working families and homegrown Oregon businesses. "We're all paying the price for these unlawful tariffs, not foreign governments," he added. Several of the affected trading partners have expressed disappointment over the new tariffs, with Brazil and Japan's governments separately calling the measures "unjustified". China's foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning described the tariffs as an "excuse for political manipulation". Washington and Beijing have been locked in a tit-for-tat tariffs war which is currently on hold. - What tariffs has Trump introduced and why? - Published17 hours ago Some analysts have also questioned how countries would be able to show that they had properly addressed the forced labour claims. The lawsuit will pose a "formidable challenge" to Trump's levies, Alex Capri, a business lecturer at the National University of Singapore told the BBC. There is also a lack of credible evidence to back claims that countries have harmed US firms by violating forced labour rules, he said. Capri added that he expects "carve outs and walk-backs to gradually take the bite out of these tariffs". The legal action marks the latest move surrounding a slew of trade policies unveiled by Trump since he returned to office in January 2025. Many of the wide-ranging duties Trump imposed on global trading partners in his so-called "Liberation Day" tariffs in April last year were struck down by the US Supreme Court. "The Supreme Court has made it clear that this administration cannot ignore the law to impose sweeping tariffs," Hochul said. The court's decision prompted tens of billions of dollars in refunds to companies that had paid the levies. The president has long argued that tariffs protect American workers and boost the US economy. The tariffs that were struck down were replaced by a temporary 10% levy on all global imports. Those tariffs expired in July. More tariffs could also be on the horizon as the US is currently investigating 16 countries over claims of manufacturing overcapacity.

item.title: EU calls for stronger borders after Ceuta migrant crossings
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cyvl84zmgyro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
EU calls for stronger borders after Ceuta migrant crossings - Published European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has called for "united action" on border security after the chaotic influx of tens of thousands of migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta last week. Spain estimates that about 69,500 migrants have now returned to Morocco, exceeding initial estimates of 50,000. The official death toll on the Spanish side of the border stands at 72, with 11 deaths on the Moroccan side. EU interior minister are holding emergency talks by video conference on Tuesday to discuss the issue. The scenes in Ceuta have strained relations among some of the EU's 27 member states. In a letter to Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, von der Leyen praised his "swift handling" of the crisis. But she added: "From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points." In response to the Ceuta crossings, Italy temporarily suspended the Schengen arrangement with Spain. The Schengen agreement eliminates border checks and now encompasses more than 450 million people and 29 countries in Europe. Finland and Denmark backed Italy's move, while Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš urged a temporary suspension of Spain's Schengen membership. In response, Sánchez said he had "serious concerns" about some European governments and pointed out that Ceuta was not part of the Schengen area. While most had shown "support and solidarity", he said other European governments had chosen to attack Spain, "driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest". In her letter to the Spanish PM, von der Leyen warned that "the protection of all our external borders is a shared European responsibility", while calling for "vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed". Tuesday's video conference will be a chance to draw "lessons" from the Ceuta episode, von der Leyen said, warning the challenges of illegal immigration require "a common European response, united action and solidarity". She urged the EU to "double down" in five areas: preventing irregular migration in the first place via cooperation with partner states; strengthening external borders; implementing early warning systems; dismantling smuggling networks and reinforcing returns. Sánchez has accused migrant traffickers of exploiting a decision recently made by the country's supreme court which constrained the government's right to immediately deport people who had arrived by sea. The country's Interior Minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, said on Saturday that the situation had almost returned to normal and the country was working on an inflatable barrier to prevent illegal migration via the water. item.title: Charity cyclist, 82, dies a day after 3,300 mile ride across Australia
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gkpwj2je9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Charity cyclist, 82, dies a day after 3,300 mile ride across Australia - Published An 82-year-old bike rider who cycled 3,300 miles (5,300km) across Australia to raise money for charity has died a day after completing the challenge. Bob Montgomery's death was "unexpected" but "peaceful", his family said in a statement on social media, just a day after he had finished what he had dubbed "One Last Ride" from Broome in Western Australia to Bowral, south-west of Sydney. He and his 18-year-old grandson had raised about A$105,000 ($74,000; £55,000) for a motor neurone disease (MND) charity with the six-week ride. It was his sixth fundraising ride in support of MND NSW, the statement said, adding that it was "a cause that was deeply personal to him". His wife of 59 years, Jenny was by his side during his "peaceful passing", his family said, adding that he was "still passionately sharing his message only hours before his passing." Montgomery and his grandson Tom Malcolm had arrived in Bowral on Sunday to "roaring applause" from his local community, the national broadcaster ABC reported. He told ABC he had been motivated by meeting people along the way and enjoying a "beer or two" at each stopover. "There's so many stories and so many people we met along the way who put their hands into their pockets to throw some cash in, which is fantastic," Montgomery was quoted as saying. He had been inspired to take on the challenge after losing a cousin to MND and had raised almost A$300,000 on his previous rides. "I have seen family and friends suffer. It's heart breaking," he wrote on his fundraising page. Malcolm had continued onto Sydney on Monday where the family had gathered once again to celebrate. But shortly after the party, Montgomery suffered a medical episode, MND NSW chief executive Liam O'Meara said. O'Meara said he was "deeply saddened" by Montgomery's death, calling him a "cherished friend and tireless supporter of MND NSW".

item.title: 'My grandmother subjected my baby to female genital mutilation behind my back'
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3r0vp7n0pro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'My grandmother subjected my baby to female genital mutilation behind my back' - Published Warning: This story contains descriptions of the practices involved in female genital mutilation In what activists are calling a milestone, Colombia last week became the first country in Latin America where female genital mutilation (FGM) is now illegal. As José Carlos Cueto reports, while the bill was passed unanimously in Colombia's Congress, it follows a long battle to eradicate the dangerous and often secretive procedure. Carla Quiñonez's daughter was just six months old when the baby's great-grandmother subjected her to female genital mutilation (FGM). Quiñonez (not her real name) says when her grandmother returned the baby to her, she had a fever and was swollen and bleeding. She cried constantly. "I confronted my grandmother, but she said it was normal and that I could not tell anyone." The nearest health centre was a long journey away, so Quiñonez's mother, a midwife, tried to ease the baby's pain with medicinal plants. She also challenged Quiñonez's grandmother. But the older woman would not listen. "She said that men make fun of women who have a clitoris." FGM in Colombia FGM involves the partial or total removal of the external female genitalia, as well as other injuries inflicted on those organs for non-medical reasons. It can cause medical complications, including haemorrhaging and infection, as well as complications later in life with periods and during childbirth. It can also make it difficult for a woman to experience sexual pleasure. The World Health Organization says that around the world more than 230 million girls and women alive today have been cut, predominantly in Africa. Quiñonez, 30, has been campaigning to eradicate the practice in Colombia - where it is still practised by members of her Emberá Indigenous community. Along with fellow activists and members of Colombia's Congress, she played a key role in the campaign which led to the ban. She says it was only as she grew up that she realised what was secretly happening within her community. "I always wondered why more girls than boys seemed to die shortly after birth. "I remember a young cousin of mine whose birth was attended by my mother. She was born healthy, but died three days later. "I asked my mother about it, and she told me the baby had died from 'jai', an ancestral illness." Quiñonez now believes that girls who supposedly died from "jai" actually died from complications related to FGM. A paediatrician's perspective Between 2020 and June 2026, 240 cases of FGM were recorded in Colombia. In the vast majority of instances, the girls were younger than six years old. But paediatrician Diana Ramos Mosquera says she believes this is just "the tip of the iceberg". Working at San Jorge University Hospital in Pereira, a city in Colombia's north-west coffee-growing region, she says she's seen signs of scarring, burning and mutilation when examining girls who have come in with other medical conditions. She recalls one girl who arrived with her vaginal opening sealed shut, meaning she probably would not have been able to menstruate or have sexual intercourse when she reached adulthood. "She had to undergo reconstructive surgery," Dr Ramos says. She regards FGM as a form of sexual and gender-based violence with lifelong consequences, but says this must be addressed through education, and not just punishment. "Some members of these communities genuinely believe they are doing no harm," she says. 'Culture does not kill' With around 300,000 members, the Great Emberá Nation is one of Colombia's largest Indigenous communities, with populations also living in Ecuador and Panama. One theory about why members of the community practise FGM, when it's rarely seen elsewhere in Latin America, is that the practice arrived with enslaved people from African countries. This could help explain its prevalence in Risaralda, Chocó and Valle del Cauca, neighbouring departments that either are home to, or border, large Afro-Colombian populations. Another theory is that the birth of an intersex child, hundreds of years ago, left the community with a fear of the clitoris - with many older women believing that it will grow into a penis if not cut. Others think that it stems from the patriarchal belief that a woman with an organ associated with sexual pleasure is more likely to be promiscuous. Whatever its origin, Juliana Domico, the legal representative and chief Indigenous councillor to the National Confederation of the Peoples of the Great Emberá Nation of Colombia, rejects the idea that the practice is cultural. "Our culture is our clothing, our crafts, our dances and our language, not a practice that kills. Culture does not kill." She says the new law follows years of advocacy work within the community: "We hope the law is translated into public policy, with sufficient resources to implement it." Threats and hostility Quiñonez is one of those who have advocated for change, but says she has received threats because of this - especially from men. While, traditionally, men are not meant to know about the ritual, conversations about abolishing the practice often only take place with male leaders because many Emberá women speak an indigenous language - also called Emberá - and have not necessarily learned Spanish. This can also prevent women from accessing help from doctors for their babies, a problem which Quiñonez says is compounded when they're faced by sometimes ill-informed and judgmental health staff. She says when she took her daughter to hospital with a fever caused by a urinary tract infection, the nurse berated her for "being a savage" and told her that she had got what she deserved. "I was even threatened with having my daughter taken away and placed in the care of the child welfare authorities. "Since then, I prefer not to take my daughter to hospital. I treat her with medicinal plants and medication. I never leave her side." 'Conversation cannot be avoided' Quiñonez says that there is change under way within the Emberá community, with women now discussing among themselves whether FGM should happen. She says she was moved when one grandmother reflected on carrying out FGM on her granddaughters. "She said she had never acted out of malice and had only wanted to prevent men from criticising her granddaughters." Having conversations about a different way of life can be painful, she says. "Women who have grown up without a clitoris cannot imagine a different body." It will also be difficult to speak to her own daughter about it, one day in the future, "but it is a conversation that cannot be avoided," she says. "All of us deserve to understand our bodies and to talk about them without shame." item.title: The avalanche that killed a climbing legend - and a generation of record-setting guides
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2ge4dnj80o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The avalanche that killed a climbing legend - and a generation of record-setting guides - Published Altogether, they summited Mount Everest dozens of times and achieved numerous feats previously thought impossible - like climbing 8,000m peaks without supplemental oxygen and scaling K2, one of the world's most lethal mountains, in the dead of winter. But beyond these accomplishments, the six Nepalis who died in an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak last week also elevated the world's recognition of Nepali mountain guides, or Sherpas, who had previously been seen as mere aides. Among those killed was the decorated British-Nepali climber Nirmal Purja, best known for climbing the world's 14 highest peaks, rising above 8,000m (26,246 ft), in just over six months. Their fellow guides say their deaths deal a devastating blow to Nepal's mountaineering community. 'Best of his generation' Purja, 43, also known as Nims, was the leading figure of the 10-member international team up Broad Peak, the world's 12th highest mountain, when the avalanche struck. "Nims of course was iconic and undisputedly amongst the best of his generation," says Ben Ayers, a longtime Everest reporter for Outside Magazine. Kili Pemba Sherpa and Pur Bahadur Gurung, who were also guiding the Broad Peak expedition, were "strong climbers with a solid resume", Ayers said. Kili Pemba, 46, had just earned the coveted mountaineering Grand Slam after completing his last of the 14 highest peaks, also known as eight-thousanders, in early July. Even before this crowning achievement, he was already among the best in the industry having been part of the Nepali team, led again by Purja, that completed the first winter ascent of K2 in January 2021. At the time, K2, the world's second highest peak, was the only one of the eight-thousanders not yet climbed in winter. But at 8,611m, K2 is known to be steeper, more unpredictable and deadlier than Everest (8,849m). Many have described Kili Pemba as humble and deeply committed in serving his clients. Two of the 15 times he summited Everest he did so guiding double-leg amputees up the mountain. "That was the toughest task for any guide, [Kili Pemba] did that with a lot of care," says Gyanendra Shrestha, a government official who was at Base Camp during one of these climbs. Pur Bahadur Gurung, 37, scaled 12 of the 14 highest peaks and was one of only 100 Nepali guides certified by the International Federation of Mountain Guides Association (IFMGA). "It takes a lot of money, passion and dedication to become an IFMGA guide. This tells us a lot about Pur Bahadur's zeal for mountaineering," says Himal Gautam, a spokesman for Nepal's tourism department. "It also speaks to the unprecedented loss we have suffered on Broad Peak," he adds. In 2024, Pur Bahadur was part of the team that discovered a century-old boot on Everest, believed to be that of British climber Andrew Irvine, who vanished on the mountain in 1924. The other three Nepali guides who perished on Broad Peak last week include Gyaljen Sherpa, best known for scaling the third-highest mountain Kanchenjunga three times in one season – a feat that some colleagues say deserves a Guinness World Record. Then there's Nima Sherpa, 36, who scaled four eight-thousanders in 2026 alone, and Nawang Thindu Sherpa, who in his 20s was among Nepal's rising generation of mountain guides. Placing Pakistan on the climbing radar Nepal's mountain guides spend each spring leading international clients up Nepal's highest mountains as guides or porters. When the monsoon comes around from June to September, some of them head towards Pakistan's far north, home to some of the world's highest peaks, including five eight-thousanders. International visitors to this rugged region are relatively few, but demand is growing. While over a million adventure travellers go to the Himalayas each year, the Karakoram mountains in Pakistan attract only about 15,000 hikers annually. Some credit Purja for bringing Pakistan onto the radar of mountaineers through his feat of scaling the 14 peaks in just over six months, which was documented in a Netflix film. "Nims' success gave many [guides] and foreigners the courage to believe that this mountaineering crown was truly possible," says Iswari Paudel, acting president of the Nepal Mountaineering Association. "This has made Pakistan a major overseas base for Nepali Sherpas. And while helping foreign climbers fulfil their dreams, many guides have themselves completed the 14 peaks," Iswari says. Ayers, the Everest reporter, says Purja helped "publicise a new era of mountaineering" which in many ways helped "democratise mountain-climbing", but also "fuelled commercialisation and risk". Because of how remote Pakistan's mountains are, it is far more challenging to organise expeditions there – a feat that only the best guides undertake, Sherpas tell the BBC. "We have to fix our own ropes, cut our steps into the ice, and set up camps as we go along," says Nima Rinji Sherpa. The 20-year-old set a new record in 2024 as the youngest mountaineer to summit the world's 14 highest peaks. "Even in an era of commercial mountaineering, we experience real, old-fashioned mountaineering [in Pakistan]," he says. But because the region is hard to access, climbers usually attempt two to three mountains per trip, which makes the itinerary very tight, Nima Rinji adds. In Nepal, by contrast, mountaineering infrastructure is well-developed. The main trekking routes towards Everest are lined with family-run lodges that offer beds, hot meals and other facilities. Emergency evacuations are also generally easier in the Himalayas, where there is an integrated network of rescue helicopters and aid outposts at high altitude, whereas the Karakoram range, being more isolated, features fewer accessible landing zones. "In the Pakistan mountains, getting the helicopters to base camp already takes a lot more effort, let alone flying them above high camps. "Therefore, the Sherpas who are capable of working in high-pressure situations, and who have diverse experiences and multiple skills are the ones who will operate in Pakistan," Nima Rinji says. The risks are part of the appeal While the Broad Peak disaster may spur calls to tighten safety standards, many believe it will do little to change high-altitude tourism. "Generally, these tragedies cause a moment of concern... but then things go back to how they were. It's difficult to say with any conviction that any accident in the mountains is 'preventable' as the inherent danger is so high... and that's part of the appeal," Ayers says. The mountaineering community is drawn to high-risk pursuits, says Medhavi Gulati, a researcher specialising in high-altitude mountaineering. "Often, it's the dangers and risk of death that attracts people," she says. The existing generation of mountain guides will continue to crave the global fame and world records that their predecessors have attained, she says. "I don't think that appeal will ever go away," she says. "We've seen disasters like this one before, and nothing changed," says expert mountaineer and writer Alan Arnette, who pointed to how an ice avalanche on Everest killed 16 Sherpas in April 2014, and the 11 climbers who died on K2 in 2008 after a massive chunk of ice broke off. "I doubt the Broad Peak incident will have a significant impact, given history. I hope I'm wrong," he says.

item.title: 'I feel like I dug my own grave': The workers caught in the AI transition
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgr7nxve05go?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'I feel like I dug my own grave': The workers caught in the AI transition - Published For 15 years, single mother Lisa made a living from content writing. She began writing straight out of college, freelanced for years and eventually followed a path taken by many young Filipinos: joining a multinational in the country's booming outsourcing industry. Lisa says she never felt the need to use artificial intelligence (AI) in her work. "I can say that I am able to do my job, I meet deadlines. In my opinion, there is no need for [AI]," she told the BBC. Eight months into her latest role, and one month before the position was due to become permanent, she was made redundant. In the months before, Lisa says a public relations agency had been tasked with producing AI-generated material that she and her colleagues were asked to edit. She says her skills were used to train the AI on the company writing style. "I feel like I dug my own grave," she says. "We were the ones who trained the artificial intelligence that replaced us." Lisa, not her real name, is one of several former outsourcing employees the BBC spoke to who asked to remain anonymous. They signed confidentiality agreements in return for severance pay, and fear that speaking publicly could hurt their chances of finding work in an industry which has a small network. Their experiences offer an insight into a question confronting emerging economies like the Philippines: what happens when AI begins to automate the jobs that helped lift millions of people into the middle classes? Building an industry Every evening around 5pm, streams of workers wearing company lanyards spill out of high-rise offices in the district of Cubao in Manila. It's one of several areas of the capital where multinational companies have premises – providing all sorts of outsourcing work including call centres, accounting, software development and marketing copy services for clients thousands of miles away. For over two decades, these business districts have symbolised one of the Philippines' biggest economic success stories. Beginning in the early 2000s, the country was promoted as an English-speaking alternative to India for what's called business process outsourcing (BPO). Successive governments offered tax incentives, invested in infrastructure and encouraged multinational companies to set up large operations. Global groups like Accenture, Concentrix and Teleperformance built sprawling campuses, employing hundreds of thousands of Filipinos. Today, the outsourcing industry employs roughly 1.9 million people, and generates $40bn (£30.1bn) in revenues every year, accounting for about 10% of the Philippines' economy. But experts say the industry is disproportionately vulnerable to the impact of AI. The International Labour Organization estimates that 12.7 million Filipinos - more than one in four workers - are employed in occupations exposed to generative AI, the highest share in South East Asia. The organisation expects many roles to change rather than disappear but the types of service jobs that people do in the Philippines leaves it particularly at risk. Jack Madrid, president of the IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines (IBPAP), admits that AI is being adopted by the sector. More than two-thirds of IBPAP's members are already running AI pilots, he says. "Agentic AI has the potential to automate at a much more accelerated pace," Madrid says. "Obviously, there's a layer of jobs that are automatable or have been automated." But he adds that the vast majority of affected workers have been redeployed within the same organisations. Madrid says any weakness in hiring reflects more than the impact of AI. "We've seen a slowdown in investment decisions on whether certain job functions or processes should be offshored," he says, pointing to slower global demand and uncertainty over how companies will ultimately deploy the technology. Even so, he acknowledges the challenge. "We cannot do enough to be prepared," he says. "The importance of reskilling" cannot be overstated. The pressure to automate Mary, another former content writer whose name we've changed, says her employer encouraged the use of AI as a productivity tool. Instead of making her job easier, she says it created additional responsibilities. "We had to edit more, fact-check more because the data AI produced was inaccurate," she says. "Technically it was more work for us." Like Lisa, she was later made redundant. Companies are under pressure to implement AI, to reduce costs and increase productivity, experts say. Teleperformance, the world's largest call centre operator and one of the Philippines' biggest private employers, has said AI offers an opportunity to augment rather than replace its workforce. The company expects AI to handle routine interactions while human agents move into more complex roles. Teleperformance has also said it plans to retrain employees. Accenture has similarly said that generative AI will reshape almost every job rather than eliminate positions. The firm has promised to invest billions of dollars in AI capabilities and workforce training. Concentrix - which is the biggest outsourcing firm in the Philippines - says its AI systems should remain under human oversight and has committed to training employees in the new technology. Some Filipino managers are uneasy about AI and want to slow down adoption, according to Paul Quintos, from the University of the Philippines-Diliman. They are concerned about how much of the domestic workforce might be displaced. "But there's tremendous pressure from foreign clients to adopt AI," he says. "It's a major cost-cutting measure." Philippine outsourcing companies compete directly with rivals in India and elsewhere for contracts from multinational corporations. Increasingly, those clients expect suppliers not only to provide cheaper labour, but also to integrate AI into the services they deliver. Despite hundreds of billions of dollars being invested globally in AI, Quintos says there is still limited evidence about how much productivity many workplace tools actually deliver. "There is a term called 'AI washing'," he says. Some layoffs are presented as being driven by AI when companies are in fact responding to weaker demand or slowing economic conditions, Quintos says. Attributing redundancies to AI, he adds, can make restructuring appear like technological progress rather than a response to market conditions. The next transition Labour groups have told the BBC that existing employment laws in the Philippines govern redundancy but offer little guidance on how companies should introduce AI into workplaces or consult employees over its use. The Philippines' outsourcing sector is also non-unionised, leaving many workers with little formal say over how new technologies are deployed. The government says that it, and the private sector have a responsibility to retrain workers, and risks falling behind competitors like India and Singapore. "To be completely honest, I think we're slightly behind. We have to catch up," says Leandro Aguirre of the Philippines Department of Information and Communications Technology. "We have to double our efforts to put our people in a position where they will not be displaced but actually thrive in this growing AI race." The government has committed to upskilling more than 300,000 outsourcing workers, but Aguirre acknowledges that the Philippines may need to rethink the economic model that helped make it an outsourcing centre. "We relied heavily on foreign direct investment," he says. "But I think we also need to focus on local talent and local companies." The ambition, he says, is to build home-grown AI companies capable of creating higher-value jobs. Aguirre rejects calls for sweeping new AI legislation, arguing that existing labour, privacy and consumer protection laws can be adapted more quickly through regulatory guidance. "The benefits of AI have to trickle down to people," he says. "It can't just benefit employers." For more than 20 years, the Philippines built one of the world's most successful outsourcing industries by selling the skills of its people to multinational companies. AI may not end that model, but it is certainly changing it, and risks leaving some workers behind. Additional reporting by Jaltson Akkanath Chummar and Regine Cabato

item.title: 'I was slut-shamed' - Indian women 'cockroach' protesters doxxed and abused
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g43l251vyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'I was slut-shamed' - Indian women 'cockroach' protesters doxxed and abused - Published Their videos lasted only a few seconds: lip-syncs, sarcastic reels and jokes filmed on the way to protests. But while thousands of young people filled social media with memes and videos mocking Prime Minister Narendra Modi during one of India's biggest anti-government protest in years, many of the women behind those posts say they have paid a heavy price for speaking out. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led movement that helped force the resignation of India's education minister, relied as much on Instagram as it did on marches. Memes, reels and viral videos became the movement's calling card, documenting everything from protest songs to the police crackdown when officers used tear gas and baton charges to stop demonstrators marching to parliament on 20 July. Delhi police said 60 protesters and 118 police personnel were injured on the day, but the CJP said the number of injured protesters was significantly higher than the official count. The posts reached hundreds of thousands of people, turning ordinary students into some of the movement's most recognisable faces. Since the protests ended, police have opened criminal cases against some protesters. But many women say another reckoning played out online. They describe rape threats, doctored images spreading on social media and strangers trawling through their photos and videos. Some cases spilled into TV debates, police complaints and political statements. Many more unfolded quietly, as young women deleted posts, locked their accounts and stopped answering calls from unknown numbers. The BBC spoke to four women and reviewed screenshots of abusive messages, posts and other material they shared. Their names have not been used to protect their identities. Content creator I'm in my mid-20s. I had been posting about the protests from the beginning, but 20 July was the first time I attended one. After the baton charge that day and the internet shutdown around the protest site, I went home and started sharing first-person accounts on Instagram. I also helped organise food, aid and volunteers. I thought I was just helping and didn't think of it as political. But the hate started almost immediately. I was slut-shamed and I was attacked for questioning the prime minister's comments, external after the protest ended. [Modi said he forgave the children who had abused him, urging society to do the same rather than punish them or drag them through the courts.] I have lost count of the number of messages I have deleted and people I have blocked. But the comments keep coming. As a content creator, I already live with this feeling of constantly being watched. Every word I say is scrutinised, mostly by men. When I first started creating content, I would block men if they made me feel uncomfortable. Over time, the algorithm started pushing my content towards more women. I believe that has shielded me from abuse compared with many other female creators. And still, this happened. My mother stopped reading the comments on my posts long ago. She said she couldn't bear the things strangers were saying about her daughter. I understood. What parent wouldn't be frightened by that? As a woman in India, you grow up with fear. You're told not to stay out late, to watch where you go, who you're with and how you'll get home. You learn early that your safety is something you must constantly think about. When you have a voice online, that fear doesn't disappear. It just follows you there. College student I am 20 years old, and this was my first protest. I went because I believed the students were standing up for something important. Before leaving the Metro station, I propped my phone against a railing and filmed a quick "fit check" [a video showing off her outfit before the protest.] "Going to get beaten by cops, guys," I joked. That's the kind of light-hearted videos I usually make. When police fired tear gas and charged protesters that afternoon, I kept filming. I was simply recording what was happening around me, as I always do. I never imagined those videos would reach far beyond my followers. I was wrong. One of them was shown on a national TV channel. Soon afterwards, my face began appearing in social media posts claiming protesters were being identified by the police. Someone even found out which college I attended. That's when I realised people weren't just attacking me online. They were trying to find me. My inbox filled with anonymous messages. Some said they would report me to the police so I would be beaten or arrested. Men called me degrading names associated with prostitution, made sexually explicit remarks, mocked my body and threatened violence. Some said I should be "taught a lesson". Others simply warned: "Your turn will come." What frightened me most wasn't the abuse itself, but what followed. Relatives and acquaintances called my parents, urging them to make me delete my videos or face the consequences. Seeing them so frightened was devastating. That's why I don't want my name published. I've since removed or archived almost all my protest videos. I worry less about what could happen to me than what they might do to my parents. Student activist I have always spoken my mind online. I'm a student activist and a Muslim, part of a religious minority in an increasingly polarised India. None of that ever frightened me. But after the CJP protests, everything changed. My Instagram account is private now. I've muted most of my other social media because the abuse has been unrelenting. Every time I look at my phone, there's another offensive comment or message or post about me. I went to the protest because I believed it was the right thing to do. I made a few satirical videos during the march. One mocked the prime minister. Others showed us singing on stage and chanting slogans. They were political, irreverent and the kind of videos I'd always made. But they spread far beyond the people I knew. One Instagram page edited a photograph to make it appear as though I was kissing a man to shame me. Another morphed my images and branded me an anti-national and a terrorist. I was also called a hijra - using the term for South Asia's transgender community as an insult - and dismissed as a paid protester. When my father, a journalist, read the comments, he panicked. He kept asking why I had spoken out. He said that once people saw my Muslim name, nothing else would matter. My parents have watched other Muslim activists investigated and arrested, and fear the same could happen to me. We live under constant dread. But I'm not going to stop speaking up. I still believe I was right to go to that protest. Now I just understand the cost much better than I did before. Student I'm a student in [the state of] West Bengal, where political discussions are an integral part of college life. I've participated in those conversations on campus for years, so I didn't think much before posting online about the protests. Although I first joined the Kolkata protest on 20 July, I'd already been helping online, organising supplies ranging from diabetic biscuits to masks for people worried about being identified. A friend and I also launched an Instagram fundraiser. But on 24 July, the police started detaining protesters in the state and we began talking about it online. That's when the hate really started. People began leaving spiteful comments on my fundraiser post; they called me a prostitute in private messages. They did not stop even after the protest had ended - and eventually I deleted the post. In the days that followed, the fear of being doxxed became real. I changed my name on social media, made my account private and blocked messages from people I didn't know. What hurt most was that none of my male friends faced the abuse I did. They expressed similar views but weren't targeted over their sexuality or subjected to insults about their mothers. I was. When it comes to women, the response quickly becomes about our gender. That's left me wondering why women can't express the same opinions as men online.

item.title: Mysterious elephant deaths in Kenya raise questions around pesticides
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx27p32jzj2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Mysterious elephant deaths in Kenya raise questions around pesticides - Published News that the recent deaths of 15 elephants may have been caused by pesticides sprayed on tomato crops surrounding Amboseli National Park has raised concerns and questions in Kenya. Last week, the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) said that some of the elephants that had died between 24 June and 24 July had shown signs of "partial paralysis" that pointed to poisoning from cyanide used in pesticides. But conservationists have told the BBC that, perhaps, is not the full story. Farmers we have spoken to in the area were also sceptical. "We have stayed with this wildlife for decades and have never experienced this," Daniel Nina, who represents some of the landowners in the area, told the BBC. "So that's why we are wondering why it is happening today." The tomato farms are found in the Kimana area, which is part of a corridor between Amboseli National Park and the Tsavo National Park in the south of Kenya. It is a vast area known as the Amboseli ecosystem, which straddles the border near Tanzania where more than 2,000 elephants move along in search of food and water. These farms thrive thanks to the streams from nearby Mount Kilimanjaro and supply markets in Kenya's capital, Nairobi, and beyond. The chief vet of Kenya's Wildlife Service, Dr Isaac Lekolool, told us that they had found traces of cyanide in samples taken from the elephants' stomachs. He says that they are not ruling out deliberate poisoning but it's impossible at this stage to tell what could have killed the elephants. "It's difficult to tell because we've not seen these kind of cases before. It is almost like a one-off, and it was within a period of about a month," Lekolool said. Their working theory is that the elephants were exposed to the toxin through pesticides sprayed on nearby tomato farms. "It could be unintentional. Maybe people are trying to do some controls of pests on their crops, and that could have been maybe a source." Pesticide problem A 2024 report by Kenyan food safety initiative Route to Food found a farmer in Kimana area using an insecticide that had an "active ingredient" that was "a chemical compound of cyanide". Wangunyu Njuguna, the author of the report, said that despite being illegal in Kenya, some toxic agrochemicals are smuggled through the border with Tanzania. "The biggest problem is we're not enforcing similar standards in the region," Njuguna said. "There is no-one checking what I go and buy across the border, so I can just go buy anything and walk through the border and no-one stops me." Highly hazardous substances are common on Kenyan farms and some have been linked to serious diseases. While regulations against illegal agrochemicals exist, there's weak enforcement and little attention paid to how they can affect animals. 'It's not adding up' However, we have spoken to several wildlife conservationists who have questioned the initial findings of Kenya's Wildlife Service. Paula Kahumbu is a world-renowned conservationist who has worked with elephants for nearly 30 years. "We haven't got enough detailed information to have confidence in this claim that it's due to pesticides in crops," Kahumbu said. "Some information has been released to the public but it's not adding up. Those elephants have to eat a huge amount to kill them." Other experts who did not want to be named said the pesticide theory was inconsistent with elephant behaviour. They said that males are more likely to raid farms as they usually take more risks than females and calves. However, only one of the 15 elephants affected was an adult male. Nina, the landowners' representative, added that unlike the latest incident, previous cases of poisoning in farms had affected zebras and antelopes, which raid the same areas. "How does cyanide kill the elephants and leave behind the zebras, antelopes and wildebeests, which are eating the grass together?" Nina asked. More BBC wildlife stories from Kenya: - 'It became one of the children' - Kenyan family on adopting orphaned cheetah cub - Published24 October 2025 - Tourist pouring beer down elephant's trunk in Kenya sparks anger - Published29 August 2025 Human-wildlife conflict has persisted for decades in communities near conservation areas across Kenya. Stephen Michael, a tomato farmer in Kimana, says elephants and giraffes occasionally raid farms in the area. "Elephants come from time to time from Tsavo and Amboseli. They destroy many farms, not just mine," Michael said. "The last time elephants came, they destroyed cabbages and tomatoes. I lost cabbages worth almost $1,535. That doesn't include tomatoes. I might start crying if I count that." Frank Pope, CEO of conservation organisation Save the Elephants, told the BBC the pressure on Amboseli's elephants isn't ivory anymore. "It's land use," he said. Farms and lodges are increasingly taking up land around the park which was previously used by elephants. It is such activities that Pope says worsen the conflict with wildlife. "People are moving into areas where there's enough water to grow crops, and fertile soils, and those are the very areas that the elephants tend to use as well." Nobody knows for sure what's causing the elephant deaths now. The fear is that the remaining elephants and the people who live near them could still be at risk. item.title: Analysis: Trump challenged by cold reality from top allies
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgjed2q2l0xo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Analysis: Trump challenged by cold reality from top allies - Published It's been a humbling few days for Donald Trump, even if the American president is reluctant to acknowledge it. In a series of setbacks, Trump has faced adversity in matters both large and small; two of which he cares about dearly and one that could determine his and his party's political fate for the remaining two years of his presidential term. From a flawed attempt to renovate a Washington landmark to questions about his pick to head the justice department to increasingly complicated efforts to end his war in Iran, the president has been handling tricky issues - many of his own making. Trump's response has been a familiar one. A first term refrain - that the president makes his own reality with "alternative facts" - is still the operative one. He sticks to beliefs even in the face of conflicting evidence. Unlike his first term, however, when many of his most notable conflicts were with dissenters in his own administration, this time around he has butted heads even with those who have proven themselves the most loyal to him. On Friday, US Attorney Jeanine Pirro, a former Fox News host and stalwart Trump ally, moved to drop felony destruction of property charges against former Olympian David Hearn, who federal prosecutors had accused of intentionally damaging the Reflecting Pool near the Washington Monument. "The damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism," she wrote in a 20-page court filing announcing her department's decision. She attributed her decision to prosecute Hearn as the result of misleading information provided by the Department of Interior. Trump may embrace alternative facts, but the evidence Pirro confronted - what she would have had to defend in court, before a judge and potentially sceptical jury - provided scarce support for her case. And so she abandoned it. Trump had enthusiastically endorsed the vandalism explanation, however, and he stuck by it. In a Truth Social post on Saturday, he criticised Pirro's decision to drop the case and did so again in comments from the Oval Office on Monday. "She folded like an umbrella," he griped. If the Reflecting Pool case was an instance of Trump being forced to face legal reality, up on Capitol Hill it was an unpleasant political reality that confronted him. One of Trump's closest allies – his former criminal defence attorney Todd Blanche – was hitting stiff headwinds in his bid to become attorney general on a permanent basis. Two Republican senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, had joined Democrats to block Blanche's nomination. They were demanding Blanche provide a letter formally disavowing any attempts to revive the proposed $1.8bn (£1.34bn) fund to pay individuals who claimed to have been the targets of politicised government prosecution. Tillis called it a "payout pot for punks" amid concerns it could be used to compensate people prosecuted over the US Capitol riot by Trump's supporters in 2021. In another Saturday Truth Social post, Trump wrote that he would keep Blanche on as acting attorney general and "push hard" to get Congress to pass legislation authorising the fund. "It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done," he wrote, suggesting that no matter what the ultimate outcome of Blanche's nomination, Trump is unlikely to ever let the issue go. The political maths in the Senate, however, was undeniable. By the next day Blanche had acceded to the senators' request, releasing two letters that Tillis and Cornyn said satisfied their concerns. In comments from the White House on Monday, Blanche escaped the scolding that Pirro the prosecutor received. Trump said he "didn't look at" Blanche's documents. "I understand there's been a sign-off, but I don't know what they agreed," he said. While the Reflecting Pool prosecution and the so-called "anti-weaponisation fund" may be topics of intense presidential interest, they barely register as concerns for the larger American public. That is decidedly not the case with the war with Iran, where Trump is once again accusing Iran of deceit amid another round of on-again, off-again negotiations and threats of overwhelming American military action. On Monday, after asserting the previous day that he had called off "an attack that would have been the biggest attack since World War II" at the behest of Iranian officials and Arab intermediaries, Trump took to Truth Social to condemn what he said was Iranian duplicity after Iran denied any new direct negotiations. "They ask for a meeting, some would say 'beg', talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they're not having any discussions," Trump wrote. If Iranians are misrepresenting the status of talks it wouldn't be the first time - but it also wouldn't be the first time Trump has seemingly taken their assurances at face value and heralded a new diplomatic breakthrough. US officials told the BBC's partner CBS News on Monday that no "new" or novel negotiations with Iran were planned. An Iranian official said the country's only current talks were with Oman, over the future of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The latest twists in the war have become a familiar pattern with little progress, as polls continue to show American disapproval of the conflict and concern that Trump is not achieving his war goals. Those recent public-opinion surveys suggest the war has become a growing drag on the president's overall popularity. A recent Associated Press poll puts Trump's approval at 33%, aligned with similar findings by CNN, Quinnipiac and YouGov. That matches or is below Trump's ratings after the Capitol riot and is above only Richard Nixon – who resigned from office in disgrace - among second-term US presidents in modern American history. Trump, however, has repeatedly dismissed surveys suggesting his historic unpopularity. "My REAL Polling Numbers, not those made up by the Fake News Media, are the best they have ever been," he posted to Truth Social on Monday. In three months, voters will head to the polls for congressional midterm elections. And Trump has shown surprising strength at the ballot box in the past, even in the face of seemingly daunting poll numbers. While Trump may be grappling with – and, at times denying - recent adversity, that will be the ultimate measure of his political fate. And if Republicans struggle, it may provide yet another reality that Trump, despite his best efforts, must eventually face. item.title: Ukrainian vegetable seller targeted in 'human safari' drone attack
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/clye173d533o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ukrainian vegetable seller targeted in 'human safari' drone attack Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared a video of a street vendor being hunted by a drone before it exploded. The man in the video verified by the BBC, 52-year-old street vegetable seller Yuriy, managed to survive the attack, but sustained shrapnel wounds and a concussion. Known by some in Ukraine as "human safari", the deployment of remotely-operated drones against civilians has often been used by Russians to terrify residents of front line areas. This particular drone attack happened in Kherson, which sits only a few miles from the front line. Russia has repeatedly denied intentionally targeting civilians. The BBC's Paul Adams reports from Kyiv. Around 400 people were evacuated from communities near the volcano and taken to temporary shelters in Alotenango and Escuintla city. Schools close to the volcano were closed due to the risk of ash fall and further volcanic activity. Emergency services urged residents to leave their homes for their safety. In 2018, a violent eruption of the Fuego volcano left hundreds dead. Fuego is just 16km (10 miles) west of Antigua, a city popular with tourists, who travel to the Unesco World Heritage Site to admire its colonial-era architecture.
